title: Θυσία ἐν Πύλῳ
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Next morning Nestor takes his seat on the polished stones before his doors, his sons gather round him with Telemachus among them, and he orders the sacrifice he vowed to Athena: a heifer from the plain, Telemachus' crew from the ship, and a goldsmith to gild the heifer's horns. The sacrifice is told step by step, from the washing of hands and the sprinkled barley to the killing, the burning of the thigh-pieces and the roasting of the meat, and the goddess herself comes to receive it. Meanwhile Nestor's youngest daughter, Polycaste, bathes Telemachus, who steps from the bath looking like one of the immortals. After the feast Nestor has horses yoked, and his son Peisistratus drives Telemachus across the plain; they spend the night at Pherae in the house of Diocles, and at dawn drive on across the wheat-bearing plain until the sun sets and Book 3 ends.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
ὤρνυτ’ ἄρ’ ἐξ εὐνῆφι Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ,
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
ōrnyt’ ar’ ex eunēphi Gerēnios hippota Nestōr,
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
up rose from his bed the Gerenian horseman Nestor,
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, the Gerenian horseman Nestor rose from his bed,
sentences.n: The first line is the dawn formula and keeps its English from 2.1; the second is built like 2.2, with Nestor where Telemachus stood there. ἦμος 'when' has no answering 'then'. φάνη is the unaugmented aorist passive of φαίνω, 'appeared': Homer's past tenses may drop the augment ἐ-. ὤρνυτ’ is ὤρνυτο, imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι 'rise'. εὐνῆφι has the old ending -φι, doing the work of a genitive after ἐξ, 'from his bed'. The meaning of Γερήνιος, Nestor's fixed epithet, is disputed. The sentence runs on to 408 with only commas, so it is cut here, with the old man up.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἐλθὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ ἐπὶ ξεστοῖσι λίθοισιν,
οἵ οἱ ἔσαν προπάροιθε θυράων ὑψηλάων,
λευκοί, ἀποστίλβοντες ἀλείφατος·
sentences.tr:
ek d’ elthōn kat’ ar’ hezet’ epi xestoisi lithoisin,
hoi hoi esan proparoithe thyraōn hypsēlaōn,
leukoi, apostilbontes aleiphatos·
sentences.i: and he came out and sat down on the polished stones that stood for him in front of the high doors, white, and glistening with oil;
sentences.n: ἐκ δ’ ἐλθών: ἐκ is an adverb, 'out'. κατ’ … ἕζετ’ is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb, for καθέζετο 'sat down'. ξεστοῖσι λίθοισιν is a dative plural in -οισι, 'polished stones', from ξέω 'scrape smooth'. In οἵ οἱ the first word is the relative and the second the enclitic dative 'for him': the stones are his seat. θυράων is a genitive plural in -άων (Attic θυρῶν). ἀλείφατος, genitive of ἄλειφαρ 'oil, unguent', gives the source of the gleam; whether the stones had actually been oiled, or only shone as if oiled, is debated.

sentences.t:
οἷς ἔπι μὲν πρὶν
Νηλεὺς ἵζεσκεν, θεόφιν μήστωρ ἀτάλαντος·
sentences.tr:
hois epi men prin
Nēleus hizesken, theophin mēstōr atalantos·
sentences.l:
on which before
Neleus used to sit, a counsellor, a match for the gods;
sentences.i: on them in former days Neleus used to sit, a counsellor to match the gods;
sentences.n: οἷς ἔπι is 'on which': the preposition follows its noun and throws its accent back. πρίν is here an adverb, 'formerly'. ἵζεσκεν has the iterative suffix -σκ-, 'used to sit', and, like most such forms, no augment. Neleus is Nestor's father. θεόφιν carries the old ending -φι(ν), here with the force of a dative after ἀτάλαντος 'equal in the balance, a match for' (from τάλαντον 'scale'). μήστωρ is 'counsellor, deviser', from μήδομαι 'devise'. μέν looks forward to Nestor, who now holds the seat.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἤδη κηρὶ δαμεὶς Ἄϊδόσδε βεβήκει,
Νέστωρ αὖ τότ’ ἐφῖζε Γερήνιος, οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν,
σκῆπτρον ἔχων.
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men ēdē kēri dameis Aïdosde bebēkei,
Nestōr au tot’ ephize Gerēnios, ouros Achaiōn,
skēptron echōn.
sentences.l:
but he already, by his doom overcome, had gone to Hades’,
and Nestor in turn now sat on them, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans,
holding a staff.
sentences.i: but he had already been overcome by his doom and gone to the house of Hades, and now Gerenian Nestor, the warden of the Achaeans, sat there in his turn, holding a staff.
sentences.n: ὁ μέν is Neleus, 'he, for his part'. κηρὶ δαμείς is 'overcome by his doom': κήρ is the death allotted to each man, and δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι 'subdue'. Ἄϊδόσδε is the genitive Ἄϊδος with -δε 'towards', 'to (the house) of Hades'. βεβήκει is pluperfect, 'had gone'. ἐφῖζε is the imperfect of ἐφίζω 'sit upon', and it is augmented: ἵζω has a short ι, and the circumflex on ῖ shows the ι lengthened, which is how a verb beginning with ι takes the augment. οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν, 'warden of the Achaeans', is a different word from οὖρος 'fair wind' and is related to ὁράω 'see, watch'.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ υἷες ἀολλέες ἠγερέθοντο
ἐκ θαλάμων ἐλθόντες, Ἐχέφρων τε Στρατίος τε
Περσεύς τ’ Ἄρητός τε καὶ ἀντίθεος Θρασυμήδης.
sentences.tr:
peri d’ huies aollees ēgerethonto
ek thalamōn elthontes, Echephrōn te Stratios te
Perseus t’ Arētos te kai antitheos Thrasymēdēs.
sentences.l:
And around him his sons all together were gathering,
from their chambers having come, Echephron and Stratius
and Perseus and Aretus and godlike Thrasymedes.
sentences.i: His sons came from their chambers and gathered round him all together, Echephron and Stratius, Perseus and Aretus and godlike Thrasymedes.
sentences.n: περί is an adverb, 'around (him)'. ἠγερέθοντο is an imperfect passive of an extended form of ἀγείρω 'gather'. υἷες is an epic nominative plural of υἱός, and ἀολλέες means 'all together, in a body'. The θάλαμοι are their own chambers in the house. The five brothers are named in a list joined by τε … τε, and only Thrasymedes, already seated beside his father at 3.39, has an epithet: ἀντίθεος 'godlike' is a general epithet of heroes and keeps its fixed English.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἔπειθ’ ἕκτος Πεισίστρατος ἤλυθεν ἥρως,
πὰρ δ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχον θεοείκελον εἷσαν ἄγοντες.
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ epeith’ hektos Peisistratos ēlythen hērōs,
par d’ ara Tēlemachon theoeikelon heisan agontes.
sentences.l:
And to them then as sixth Peisistratus came, the hero,
and beside them then Telemachus, the god-resembling, they seated, leading him.
sentences.i: Then Peisistratus the hero came to join them as the sixth, and they brought Telemachus, who was like a god, and seated him beside them.
sentences.n: τοῖσι is a pronoun, 'to them'. ἔπειθ’ is ἔπειτα, with τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ἕκτος: Peisistratus makes the sixth son. ἤλυθεν is an epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (= ἦλθεν), and ἥρως 'the hero' is a title of rank. πάρ is παρά shortened, an adverb, 'beside (them)'. εἷσαν is the aorist of ἵζω in its causative sense, 'made to sit, seated'. θεοείκελος, from θεός and εἴκελος 'like', is 'god-resembling', an epithet kept apart from θεοειδής 'godlike in form'.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: The Gerenian horseman Nestor was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is the pronoun in the dative, 'among them'. ἄρχω takes a genitive of what is begun, so μύθων ἦρχε is 'began the speaking': Nestor is the first to speak. The line is a speech-introduction built like 1.28, where Zeus speaks, and like 3.68, which has τοῖς ἄρα in place of τοῖσι δέ; it comes back at 474 in this part with the same English.

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως μοι, τέκνα φίλα, κρηήνατ’ ἐέλδωρ,
ὄφρ’ ἦ τοι πρώτιστα θεῶν ἱλάσσομ’ Ἀθήνην,
ἥ μοι ἐναργὴς ἦλθε θεοῦ ἐς δαῖτα θάλειαν.
sentences.tr:
karpalimōs moi, tekna phila, krēēnat’ eeldōr,
ophr’ ē toi prōtista theōn hilassom’ Athēnēn,
hē moi enargēs ēlthe theou es daita thaleian.
sentences.l:
“Quickly for me, dear children, fulfil my wish,
so that, first of the gods, I may propitiate Athena,
who to me in manifest form came, at the god’s abundant feast.
sentences.i: “Quickly, my dear children, fulfil my wish, so that before all the other gods I may win the favour of Athena, who came to me in manifest form at the god’s abundant feast.
sentences.n: καρπαλίμως is 'quickly'. κρηήνατ’ is κρηήνατε, aorist imperative of κραιαίνω 'fulfil, accomplish', and ἐέλδωρ is 'wish, desire'. ὄφρα 'so that' takes the subjunctive ἱλάσσομ’, that is ἱλάσσομαι, an aorist subjunctive with the short vowel of the epic subjunctive, from ἱλάσκομαι 'propitiate'. ἦ τοι adds emphasis. ἐναργής is 'plain to see, in manifest form'. θεοῦ … δαῖτα θάλειαν is Poseidon's feast on the shore, where Athena arrived with Telemachus; θάλεια, from θάλλω 'flourish', is 'abundant'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ὁ μὲν πεδίονδ’ ἐπὶ βοῦν, ἴτω, ὄφρα τάχιστα
ἔλθῃσιν, ἐλάσῃ δὲ βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ·
sentences.tr:
all’ ag’ ho men pediond’ epi boun, itō, ophra tachista
elthēisin, elasēi de boōn epiboukolos anēr·
sentences.l:
But come, let one to the plain, for a heifer, go, so that most quickly
she may come, and drive her may the man who herds the cattle;
sentences.i: But come, let one of you go to the plain for a heifer, so that she may come here as quickly as can be, and the herdsman who has charge of the cattle may drive her in;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ is 'but come', a call to action. ὁ μέν … εἷς δ’ … εἷς δ’ … οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι parcels out the tasks: 'one … another … another … the rest'. ἴτω is the third-person imperative of εἶμι 'go', and πεδίονδ’ has -δε 'to the plain'. βοῦν is the heifer vowed at 382. ἔλθῃσιν is an epic subjunctive in -ῃσι after ὄφρα, and ἐλάσῃ, from ἐλαύνω 'drive', continues the same purpose clause. ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ is 'the man set over the cattle'.

sentences.t:
εἷς δ’ ἐπὶ Τηλεμάχου μεγαθύμου νῆα μέλαιναν
πάντας ἰὼν ἑτάρους ἀγέτω, λιπέτω δὲ δύ’ οἴους·
sentences.tr:
heis d’ epi Tēlemachou megathymou nēa melainan
pantas iōn hetarous agetō, lipetō de dy’ oious·
sentences.l:
and let one, to great-hearted Telemachus’ black ship
going, all his companions bring, and let him leave two only;
sentences.i: let another go to the black ship of great-hearted Telemachus and bring all his companions, leaving only two behind;
sentences.n: εἷς δ’ is 'and another'. ἐπί with the accusative νῆα is 'to the ship', and ἰών is the present participle of εἶμι 'go'. μεγάθυμος 'great-hearted' keeps its fixed English. ἀγέτω and λιπέτω are third-person imperatives, 'let him bring, let him leave'. δύ’ οἴους is 'two alone': two men are to stay and guard the ship while the rest come up to the sacrifice.

sentences.t:
εἷς δ’ αὖ χρυσοχόον Λαέρκεα δεῦρο κελέσθω
ἐλθεῖν, ὄφρα βοὸς χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύῃ.
sentences.tr:
heis d’ au chrysochoon Laerkea deuro kelesthō
elthein, ophra boos chryson kerasin pericheuēi.
sentences.l:
and let one in turn the goldsmith Laerces hither bid
to come, so that gold round the heifer’s horns he may pour.
sentences.i: and let another bid Laerces the goldsmith come here, so that he may overlay the heifer’s horns with gold.
sentences.n: χρυσοχόος, literally 'gold-pourer', is a goldsmith; this one is named Laerces. κελέσθω is a third-person present imperative of κέλομαι 'bid', with the infinitive ἐλθεῖν. δεῦρο is 'hither'. βοός is the genitive of βοῦς, and κέρασιν a dative plural of κέρας 'horn'. περιχεύῃ is an aorist subjunctive of περιχέω 'pour round': the gold is beaten thin and laid round the horns, as Nestor promised the goddess at 384.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι μένετ’ αὐτοῦ ἀολλέες, εἴπατε δ’ εἴσω
δμῳῇσιν κατὰ δώματ’ ἀγακλυτὰ δαῖτα πένεσθαι,
ἕδρας τε ξύλα τ’ ἀμφὶ καὶ ἀγλαὸν οἰσέμεν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alloi menet’ autou aollees, eipate d’ eisō
dmōiēisin kata dōmat’ agaklyta daita penesthai,
hedras te xyla t’ amphi kai aglaon oisemen hydōr.
sentences.l:
And you others, stay here all together, and tell, within,
the serving-women through the renowned halls a feast to prepare,
and seats and firewood round about, and splendid water to bring.”
sentences.i: The rest of you stay here together, and tell the serving-women inside to prepare a feast throughout the renowned halls, and to bring seats and firewood to set round about, and splendid water.”
sentences.n: The orders move from third-person imperatives to the second person, μένετ’ 'stay' and εἴπατε 'tell', with οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι as the address, 'you others'. αὐτοῦ is the adverb 'here'. δμῳῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσι of δμῳή 'serving-woman, slave-woman'. πένεσθαι is 'busy oneself about, prepare'. ἀμφί is an adverb, 'round about'. οἰσέμεν is an epic infinitive of φέρω 'bring', built on the stem of the future οἴσω. ἀγλαός 'splendid' keeps its fixed English even of water, where it names brightness.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐποίπνυον.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes epoipnyon.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then, all of them, bustled about.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all of them set busily to work.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ὣς ἔφατο 'so he spoke', the regular close of a speech; the τ of the elided ἔφατο becomes θ before the rough breathing of οἱ. οἱ is the pronoun, 'they'. ἐποίπνυον is the imperfect of ποιπνύω 'bustle, be busy', a reduplicated verb used of people hurrying at a task. The sentence ends in mid-line, and the next begins a run of arrivals.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε μὲν ἂρ βοῦς
ἐκ πεδίου, ἦλθον δὲ θοῆς παρὰ νηὸς ἐίσης
Τηλεμάχου ἕταροι μεγαλήτορος,
sentences.tr:
ēlthe men ar bous
ek pediou, ēlthon de thoēs para nēos eisēs
Tēlemachou hetaroi megalētoros,
sentences.l:
Came, then, the heifer
from the plain, and came from the swift, well-balanced ship
the companions of great-spirited Telemachus,
sentences.i: The heifer came from the plain, and the companions of great-spirited Telemachus came from the swift, well-balanced ship,
sentences.n: ἦλθε … ἦλθον … ἦλθε … ἦλθε: four clauses open with the same verb and bring in, one after another, the heifer, the crew, the smith and, last, the goddess. ἂρ is ἄρα. θοῆς … νηὸς ἐίσης keeps the fixed 'swift' and 'well-balanced'; νηός is the epic genitive of ναῦς. μεγαλήτορος, from μέγας and ἦτορ 'heart, spirit', is kept distinct from μεγάθυμος at 423. The sentence runs to 435 with only commas, so it is cut here, where the crew gives way to the smith.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε δὲ χαλκεὺς
ὅπλ’ ἐν χερσὶν ἔχων χαλκήια, πείρατα τέχνης,
ἄκμονά τε σφῦράν τ’ ἐυποίητόν τε πυράγρην,
οἷσίν τε χρυσὸν εἰργάζετο·
sentences.tr:
ēlthe de chalkeus
hopl’ en chersin echōn chalkēia, peirata technēs,
akmona te sphyran t’ eypoiēton te pyragrēn,
hoisin te chryson eirgazeto·
sentences.l:
and came the smith,
the tools in his hands holding, the bronze ones, the ends of his craft,
anvil and hammer and well-made fire-tongs,
with which he worked the gold;
sentences.i: and the smith came, holding in his hands his bronze tools, the means that bring his craft to completion, anvil and hammer and well-made tongs, with which he worked the gold;
sentences.n: χαλκεύς, properly a bronze-smith, is any smith, here the goldsmith Laerces, and his tools are χαλκήια 'of bronze'. ὅπλ’ is ὅπλα 'tools'. πείρατα τέχνης is literally 'the ends of his craft', usually explained as the tools that bring the craft to completion, though the exact sense of πεῖραρ here is not certain. πυράγρη, 'fire-taker', is a pair of tongs. οἷσίν τε is a relative with epic τε. εἰργάζετο is the imperfect of ἐργάζομαι, whose augment shows as εἰ- because the verb once began with ϝ.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε δ’ Ἀθήνη
ἱρῶν ἀντιόωσα.
sentences.tr:
ēlthe d’ Athēnē
hirōn antioōsa.
sentences.l:
and came Athena
to partake of the sacred-rites.
sentences.i: and Athena came, to partake of the sacred rites.
sentences.n: The fourth arrival is the goddess herself. ἱρῶν is Ionic for ἱερῶν, 'of the sacred rites'. ἀντιόωσα is the present participle of ἀντιάω 'come to meet, partake of', with the vowel stretched out (Attic ἀντιῶσα), and it takes a genitive. The same verb was used at 1.25 of Poseidon going to share the Ethiopians' hecatomb. The narrator states her presence plainly and does not say that anyone at the rite sees her.

sentences.t:
γέρων δ’ ἱππηλάτα Νέστωρ
χρυσὸν ἔδωχ’·
sentences.tr:
gerōn d’ hippēlata Nestōr
chryson edōch’·
sentences.l:
And the old man, horse-driver Nestor,
the gold gave;
sentences.i: And Nestor, the old horse-driver, gave the gold;
sentences.n: γέρων 'old man' stands in apposition to Nestor. ἱππηλάτα, from ἵππος and ἐλαύνω 'drive', is 'horse-driver', a nominative in short -α like ἱππότα; it is kept distinct from ἱππότα 'horseman' and ἱππόδαμος 'horse-taming'. ἔδωχ’ is ἔδωκε, elided, with κ turned to χ before the rough breathing of ὁ. The king supplies the gold, and the smith does the work.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα βοὸς κέρασιν περίχευεν
ἀσκήσας, ἵν’ ἄγαλμα θεὰ κεχάροιτο ἰδοῦσα.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epeita boos kerasin pericheuen
askēsas, hin’ agalma thea kecharoito idousa.
sentences.l:
and he then round the heifer’s horns poured it,
having worked it with skill, so that the offering the goddess might rejoice to see.
sentences.i: and he then worked it with skill and overlaid the heifer’s horns with it, so that the goddess might see the offering and rejoice in it.
sentences.n: ὁ is the smith. περίχευεν is the unaugmented aorist of περιχέω, carrying out the order περιχεύῃ at 426. ἀσκήσας is 'having worked it with skill'. ἄγαλμα is 'a thing that delights', an ornament or offering for a god, and is the object of ἰδοῦσα 'seeing'. κεχάροιτο is a reduplicated aorist optative of χαίρω 'rejoice': after a past main verb, the purpose clause with ἵνα takes the optative. θεά is the usual epic word for 'goddess'.

sentences.t: βοῦν δ’ ἀγέτην κεράων Στρατίος καὶ δῖος Ἐχέφρων.
sentences.tr: boun d’ agetēn keraōn Stratios kai dios Echephrōn.
sentences.l: And the heifer they led by the horns, Stratius and heavenly Echephron.
sentences.i: Stratius and heavenly Echephron led the heifer by the horns.
sentences.n: ἀγέτην is a dual imperfect of ἄγω, unaugmented (Attic ἠγέτην): two brothers, a horn each. κεράων is an uncontracted genitive plural of κέρας, 'by the horns', a genitive of the part taken hold of. δῖος 'heavenly' keeps its fixed English even for a figure as minor as Echephron: it is a general honorific, not a special claim for him.

sentences.t:
χέρνιβα δέ σφ’ Ἄρητος ἐν ἀνθεμόεντι λέβητι
ἤλυθεν ἐκ θαλάμοιο φέρων, ἑτέρῃ δ’ ἔχεν οὐλὰς
ἐν κανέῳ πέλεκυν δὲ μενεπτόλεμος Θρασυμήδης
ὀξὺν ἔχων ἐν χειρὶ παρίστατο βοῦν ἐπικόψων.
sentences.tr:
cherniba de sph’ Arētos en anthemoenti lebēti
ēlythen ek thalamoio pherōn, heterēi d’ echen oulas
en kaneōi pelekyn de meneptolemos Thrasymēdēs
oxyn echōn en cheiri paristato boun epikopsōn.
sentences.l:
And hand-water for them Aretus, in a flowered basin,
came from the chamber bringing, and in the other hand he held barley-grains
in a basket; and the axe, steadfast-in-battle Thrasymedes,
sharp, holding in his hand, stood by, to strike the heifer.
sentences.i: Aretus came from the chamber bringing them water for their hands in a basin worked with flowers, and in his other hand he held the barley-grains in a basket; and Thrasymedes, steadfast in battle, stood by with a sharp axe in his hand, ready to strike the heifer.
sentences.n: χέρνιβα is 'water for washing the hands', with which the rite begins. σφ’ is σφι 'for them'. ἀνθεμόεντι, 'flowered', describes a basin decorated with flowers, and a λέβης is a cauldron or basin. ἑτέρῃ (with χειρί understood) is 'in his other hand'. οὐλαί are whole barley-grains to be thrown on the victim, carried in a κάνεον 'basket'. Murray prints no comma after κανέῳ. μενεπτόλεμος is 'steadfast in battle', from μένω 'stand fast' and πόλεμος. ἐπικόψων is a future participle of purpose, 'to strike'.

sentences.t: Περσεὺς δ’ ἀμνίον εἶχε·
sentences.tr: Perseus d’ amnion eiche·
sentences.l: And Perseus held the blood-bowl;
sentences.i: Perseus held the bowl for the blood;
sentences.n: Perseus has the last of the tasks. ἀμνίον occurs only here in Homer, and its meaning rests on ancient explanation: a bowl to catch the blood of the victim, which is how it is taken here. εἶχε is the imperfect of ἔχω, with the augment contracted into the stem. With all five brothers at their tasks, the old king begins the rite.

sentences.t:
γέρων δ’ ἱππηλάτα Νέστωρ
χέρνιβά τ’ οὐλοχύτας τε κατήρχετο, πολλὰ δ’ Ἀθήνῃ
εὔχετ’ ἀπαρχόμενος, κεφαλῆς τρίχας ἐν πυρὶ βάλλων.
sentences.tr:
gerōn d’ hippēlata Nestōr
cherniba t’ oulochytas te katērcheto, polla d’ Athēnēi
euchet’ aparchomenos, kephalēs trichas en pyri ballōn.
sentences.l:
and the old man, horse-driver Nestor,
with hand-water and barley-for-sprinkling began the rite, and much to Athena
he prayed, as he made the first offering, hairs of the head casting into the fire.
sentences.i: and Nestor, the old horse-driver, began the rite with the hand-water and the barley for sprinkling, and as he made the first offering, casting hairs from the heifer’s head into the fire, he prayed long to Athena.
sentences.n: κατήρχετο is the imperfect of κατάρχομαι 'begin (a sacrifice) with', taking the accusatives χέρνιβα 'hand-water' and οὐλοχύτας 'barley for sprinkling' (from οὐλαί and χέω 'pour'). πολλά is adverbial, 'much, earnestly', and εὔχετ’ is εὔχετο 'prayed'. ἀπαρχόμενος is 'making the first offering': hairs are cut from the victim's head and thrown into the fire, and κεφαλῆς τρίχας … βάλλων says just that. The Greek does not say whose head; it is the heifer's.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ εὔξαντο καὶ οὐλοχύτας προβάλοντο,
αὐτίκα Νέστορος υἱὸς ὑπέρθυμος Θρασυμήδης
ἤλασεν ἄγχι στάς·
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ euxanto kai oulochytas probalonto,
autika Nestoros huios hyperthymos Thrasymēdēs
ēlasen anchi stas·
sentences.i: But when they had prayed and thrown down the barley for sprinkling, Nestor’s son, high-spirited Thrasymedes, at once stepped close and struck;
sentences.n: ῥ’ is ῥα. εὔξαντο is the aorist of εὔχομαι 'pray'. προβάλοντο is an unaugmented aorist middle, 'threw forward', of the barley cast onto the victim. ὑπέρθυμος, from ὑπέρ and θυμός, is 'high-spirited, of overflowing spirit'; it is not a reproach. ἤλασεν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω in its sense 'strike, deal a blow'. ἄγχι στάς is 'standing close', with στάς the aorist participle of ἵστημι.

sentences.t:
πέλεκυς δ’ ἀπέκοψε τένοντας
αὐχενίους, λῦσεν δὲ βοὸς μένος.
sentences.tr:
pelekys d’ apekopse tenontas
auchenious, lysen de boos menos.
sentences.l:
and the axe cut through the sinews
of the neck, and loosed the heifer’s strength.
sentences.i: the axe cut through the sinews of the neck and loosed the heifer’s strength.
sentences.n: πέλεκυς is the axe Thrasymedes held at 442. ἀπέκοψε is the aorist of ἀποκόπτω 'cut off, cut through'. τένοντας αὐχενίους are the sinews of the neck: the blow severs them and the animal drops. λῦσεν is an unaugmented aorist of λύω, and 'loosed her strength' is the Homeric way of saying that the force has gone out of a living body. The throat is cut a few lines later, at 454.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ὀλόλυξαν
θυγατέρες τε νυοί τε καὶ αἰδοίη παράκοιτις
Νέστορος, Εὐρυδίκη, πρέσβα Κλυμένοιο θυγατρῶν.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ ololyxan
thygateres te nyoi te kai aidoiē parakoitis
Nestoros, Eurydikē, presba Klymenoio thygatrōn.
sentences.l:
And the women raised the cry,
the daughters and the daughters-in-law and the revered wife
of Nestor, Eurydice, eldest of the daughters of Clymenus.
sentences.i: And the women raised their cry, Nestor’s daughters and his sons’ wives and his revered wife Eurydice, the eldest of the daughters of Clymenus.
sentences.n: ὀλόλυξαν is an unaugmented aorist of ὀλολύζω, the shrill cry that women raise at the moment of the sacrificial blow. νυοί are daughters-in-law, the wives of Nestor's sons. αἰδοίη 'revered' keeps its fixed English, and παράκοιτις is 'bedfellow, wife'. Line 451 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρες, naturally short, has to be lengthened to make the first foot (καί shortened before αἰδοίη is ordinary epic correption). πρέσβα is taken here as 'eldest', with the partitive genitive θυγατρῶν, but the word is also a title of honour, 'august', and 'first in rank among the daughters' is possible.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀνελόντες ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης
ἔσχον·
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeit’ anelontes apo chthonos euryodeiēs
eschon·
sentences.l:
Then they, having lifted her from the wide-wayed earth,
held her;
sentences.i: Then the men lifted the heifer from the wide-wayed earth and held her;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν is 'they', the men, set against Peisistratus in the next clause. ἀνελόντες is the aorist participle of ἀναιρέω 'take up, lift', and ἔσχον the aorist of ἔχω, 'held': the fallen animal is raised from the ground and held for the stroke that follows. χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης is 'the wide-wayed earth', an epithet of the earth that bears the roads. The sentence ends after the first word of line 454.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ σφάξεν Πεισίστρατος, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr: atar sphaxen Peisistratos, orchamos andrōn.
sentences.l: and then cut her throat Peisistratus, chief of men.
sentences.i: and Peisistratus, chief of men, cut her throat.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is a by-form of αὐτάρ, 'but, and then'. σφάξεν is an unaugmented aorist of σφάζω 'cut the throat': this is the killing stroke, after the stunning blow at 449. Peisistratus, who took the guests by the hand on the shore and slept beside Telemachus in the portico, has his share of the rite as well. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν 'chief of men' keeps its fixed English.

sentences.t:
τῆς δ’ ἐπεὶ ἐκ μέλαν αἷμα ῥύη, λίπε δ’ ὀστέα θυμός,
αἶψ’ ἄρα μιν διέχευαν, ἄφαρ δ’ ἐκ μηρία τάμνον
πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν, κατά τε κνίσῃ ἐκάλυψαν
δίπτυχα ποιήσαντες, ἐπ’ αὐτῶν δ’ ὠμοθέτησαν.
sentences.tr:
tēs d’ epei ek melan haima rhyē, lipe d’ ostea thymos,
aips’ ara min diecheuan, aphar d’ ek mēria tamnon
panta kata moiran, kata te knisēi ekalypsan
diptycha poiēsantes, ep’ autōn d’ ōmothetēsan.
sentences.l:
And when from her the black blood had flowed out, and the spirit had left her bones,
quickly then they cut her apart, and at once the thigh-pieces they cut out,
all according to what is fitting, and covered them over with fat,
making it double-folded, and on them they laid raw pieces.
sentences.i: And when the black blood had flowed out of her and the spirit had left her bones, they quickly cut her up and at once cut out the thigh-pieces, all as is fitting, covered them with fat folded double, and laid raw morsels on them.
sentences.n: τῆς is 'from her', the heifer. ἐκ … ῥύη is tmesis of ἐκρέω, with the unaugmented aorist passive ῥύη 'flowed'. λίπε is an unaugmented aorist of λείπω, and θυμός, the spirit of life, is its subject. διέχευαν, literally 'poured apart', is 'cut up'. ἐκ … τάμνον is tmesis again; τάμνω is epic for τέμνω. The μηρία, the thigh-pieces, are the god's portion. κατά … ἐκάλυψαν is a third tmesis: the thigh-pieces are wrapped in a double fold of fat (κνίση), and raw morsels are laid on top (ὠμοθέτησαν, from ὠμός 'raw' and τίθημι 'place').

sentences.t:
καῖε δ’ ἐπὶ σχίζῃς ὁ γέρων, ἐπὶ δ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον
λεῖβε·
sentences.tr:
kaie d’ epi schizēis ho gerōn, epi d’ aithopa oinon
leibe·
sentences.l:
And he burned them on split wood, the old man, and over them the fire-faced wine
poured;
sentences.i: The old man burned them on split wood and poured the wine that has the look of fire over them;
sentences.n: καῖε and λεῖβε are unaugmented imperfects, 'burned' and 'poured'. σχίζῃς is a dative plural in -ῃς (Attic -αις) of σχίζα 'split wood', the fuel of the altar-fire. ὁ γέρων 'the old man' is the narrator's name for Nestor. ἐπί in both clauses is an adverb, 'upon (them)'. αἴθοπα οἶνον keeps its fixed English: the wine is poured over the burning offering as a libation.

sentences.t: νέοι δὲ παρ’ αὐτὸν ἔχον πεμπώβολα χερσίν.
sentences.tr: neoi de par’ auton echon pempōbola chersin.
sentences.l: and young men beside him held five-pronged forks in their hands.
sentences.i: and beside him young men held five-pronged forks in their hands.
sentences.n: νέοι is 'young men', helpers at the rite. ἔχον is an unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω. πεμπώβολα are five-pronged forks, from Aeolic πέμπε 'five' (Attic πέντε) and ὀβελός 'spit'; on them the entrails were held in the fire to roast. χερσίν is a dative plural of χείρ 'hand'. παρ’ αὐτόν, with the accusative, is 'beside him'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ μῆρ’ ἐκάη καὶ σπλάγχνα πάσαντο,
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρα τἆλλα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειραν,
ὤπτων δ’ ἀκροπόρους ὀβελοὺς ἐν χερσὶν ἔχοντες.
sentences.tr:
autar epei kata mēr’ ekaē kai splanchna pasanto,
mistyllon t’ ara talla kai amph’ obeloisin epeiran,
ōptōn d’ akroporous obelous en chersin echontes.
sentences.l:
But when the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails,
they cut up the rest then into pieces and pierced them around spits,
and roasted them, the sharp-pointed spits in their hands holding.
sentences.i: But when the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails, they cut up the rest into small pieces, pierced them on spits, and roasted them, holding the sharp-pointed spits in their hands.
sentences.n: With the god's portion burned, the rest of the animal becomes the meal. κατὰ … ἐκάη is tmesis of κατακαίω, with the aorist passive ἐκάη 'were burned up'. μῆρ’ is μῆρα, a by-form of μηρία. πάσαντο is the unaugmented aorist of πατέομαι 'taste'. μίστυλλον 'cut into small pieces' is an unaugmented imperfect. τἆλλα is crasis of τὰ ἄλλα, 'the rest'. ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειραν is literally 'pierced around spits'. ὤπτων, from ὀπτάω 'roast', keeps its augment. ἀκροπόρους is 'piercing with the point, sharp-pointed'.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ Τηλέμαχον λοῦσεν καλὴ Πολυκάστη,
Νέστορος ὁπλοτάτη θυγάτηρ Νηληϊάδαο.
sentences.tr:
tophra de Tēlemachon lousen kalē Polykastē,
Nestoros hoplotatē thygatēr Nēlēïadao.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile beautiful Polycaste bathed Telemachus,
Nestor’s youngest daughter, of Neleus’ son.
sentences.i: Meanwhile beautiful Polycaste, the youngest daughter of Nestor son of Neleus, bathed Telemachus.
sentences.n: τόφρα 'meanwhile' sets this scene beside the roasting. λοῦσεν is an unaugmented aorist of λούω 'bathe'. Polycaste is Nestor's youngest daughter: ὁπλοτάτη is the superlative of ὁπλότερος 'younger', whose sense is clear though its origin is not. Νηληϊάδαο is the patronymic 'son of Neleus', a genitive in -αο (Attic -ου) agreeing with Νέστορος. A daughter of the house bathing a guest is ordinary hospitality, not a sign of anything more.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ λοῦσέν τε καὶ ἔχρισεν λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν φᾶρος καλὸν βάλεν ἠδὲ χιτῶνα,
ἔκ ῥ’ ἀσαμίνθου βῆ δέμας ἀθανάτοισιν ὁμοῖος·
sentences.tr:
autar epei lousen te kai echrisen lip’ elaiōi,
amphi de min pharos kalon balen ēde chitōna,
ek rh’ asaminthou bē demas athanatoisin homoios·
sentences.i: But when she had bathed him and anointed him richly with oil, and thrown a fine cloak and a tunic about him, he stepped out of the bath, in body like the immortals;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί 'but when' covers three acts of Polycaste's before the main clause at ἔκ ῥ’. ἔχρισεν is the aorist of χρίω 'anoint'. λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ is 'richly with olive oil': λίπα is taken as an adverb, 'thickly, richly', though it may instead be an elided case-form of a noun 'fat' (compare λίπος). ἀμφὶ … βάλεν is tmesis, 'threw about (him)'. The φᾶρος is a large cloak, the χιτών the tunic worn beneath it. ἀσάμινθος is a bathtub. δέμας is an accusative of respect, 'in body', and ὁμοῖος 'like' takes the dative.

sentences.t: πὰρ δ’ ὅ γε Νέστορ’ ἰὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο, ποιμένα λαῶν.
sentences.tr: par d’ ho ge Nestor’ iōn kat’ ar’ hezeto, poimena laōn.
sentences.l: and beside Nestor he, going, sat down, the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: and he went and sat down beside Nestor, the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: πάρ is παρά, governing Νέστορ’ (Νέστορα, elided). ὅ γε is the pronoun 'he', Telemachus. ἰών is the participle of εἶμι 'go', and κατ’ … ἕζετο is the same tmesis as at 406, 'sat down'. ποιμένα λαῶν, 'the shepherd of the people', stands in apposition to Nestor and is a fixed title of kings. The guest, bathed and dressed, takes his place beside the host.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ ὤπτησαν κρέ’ ὑπέρτερα καὶ ἐρύσαντο,
δαίνυνθ’ ἑζόμενοι·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei ōptēsan kre’ hypertera kai erysanto,
dainynth’ hezomenoi·
sentences.l:
And they, when they had roasted the outer meat and drawn it off,
were feasting, seated;
sentences.i: And when they had roasted the outer flesh and drawn it off the spits, they sat and feasted;
sentences.n: The first line is the same as 3.65 and keeps its English. ὤπτησαν, aorist of ὀπτάω 'roast', keeps its augment. κρέ’ ὑπέρτερα, 'the upper meat', is the outer flesh, as against the entrails already tasted. ἐρύσαντο is 'drew (it) off' the spits. δαίνυνθ’ is δαίνυντο, an unaugmented imperfect of δαίνυμι 'feast', with τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ἑζόμενοι 'seated'. At 3.66 the same line ran on differently.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ἀνέρες ἐσθλοὶ ὄροντο
οἶνον οἰνοχοεῦντες ἐνὶ χρυσέοις δεπάεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
epi d’ aneres esthloi oronto
oinon oinochoeuntes eni chryseois depaessin.
sentences.l:
and over them noble men kept watch,
wine pouring out into golden cups.
sentences.i: and noble men waited on them, pouring the wine into golden cups.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ὄροντο: LSJ takes ὄροντο from ὄρομαι 'watch over, have charge of', the root of οὖρος 'warden' at 411, so the men 'kept watch over' the diners, that is, waited on them; it is an unaugmented imperfect (the augment would give ὠρ-). Some take it instead from ὄρνυμι, 'rose (to serve)'. ἀνέρες is an epic form of ἄνδρες, and ἐσθλοί 'noble' says they are men of standing. οἰνοχοεῦντες is from οἰνοχοέω 'pour wine', with Ionic -ευ- where Attic contracts to -ου-. ἐνί is ἐν. δεπάεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι of δέπας 'cup'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
toisi de mythōn ērche Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
and among them of speeches made-beginning the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, the Gerenian horseman Nestor was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: The first line is the formula for the end of a meal and keeps the English it has at 1.150 and 3.67; the second is the same as 417 and keeps its English. ἐξ … ἕντο is tmesis of ἐξίημι 'send out, put away', with ἔρον 'desire' as its object; πόσιος and ἐδητύος, 'drink' and 'food', depend on ἔρον. The δέ that opens the main clause after an ἐπεί-clause marks the apodosis, and the reading English leaves it out.

sentences.t:
παῖδες ἐμοί, ἄγε Τηλεμάχῳ καλλίτριχας ἵππους
ζεύξαθ’ ὑφ’ ἅρματ’ ἄγοντες, ἵνα πρήσσῃσιν ὁδοῖο.
sentences.tr:
paides emoi, age Tēlemachōi kallitrichas hippous
zeuxath’ hyph’ harmat’ agontes, hina prēssēisin hodoio.
sentences.l:
“My sons, come, for Telemachus fair-maned horses
yoke beneath the chariot, bringing them, so that he may make headway on his road.”
sentences.i: “My sons, come, bring fair-maned horses for Telemachus and yoke them to the chariot, so that he may make headway on his road.”
sentences.n: παῖδες ἐμοί is 'my sons'. ἄγε is the singular 'come!', used as a fixed word even when a group is addressed. καλλίτριχας is 'fair-maned', from καλός and θρίξ 'hair'. ζεύξαθ’ is ζεύξατε, aorist imperative, with τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ὑφ’. ἅρματ’ is a plural for a single chariot. πρήσσῃσιν is an epic subjunctive in -ῃσι of πρήσσω (Attic πράττω), with the partitive genitive ὁδοῖο 'of the road': 'get on with his journey'.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδ’ ἐπίθοντο,
καρπαλίμως δ’ ἔζευξαν ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν ὠκέας ἵππους.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara tou mala men klyon ēd’ epithonto,
karpalimōs d’ ezeuxan hyph’ harmasin ōkeas hippous.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed,
and quickly yoked beneath the chariot the swift horses.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed, and quickly yoked the swift horses to the chariot.
sentences.n: τοῦ, a genitive, is the object of κλύον 'heard', an unaugmented aorist, and μάλα μέν is 'readily, very well'. ἐπίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθω, 'obeyed', and its ἐ- is the augment (unaugmented πίθοντο). καρπαλίμως 'quickly' picks up the first word of Nestor's speech at 418. ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν is 'beneath the chariot', again a plural for one vehicle. ὠκέας is from ὠκύς 'swift', the adjective in ὠκύμοροι 'swift-doomed' (1.266).

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ γυνὴ ταμίη σῖτον καὶ οἶνον ἔθηκεν
ὄψα τε, οἷα ἔδουσι διοτρεφέες βασιλῆες.
sentences.tr:
en de gynē tamiē siton kai oinon ethēken
opsa te, hoia edousi diotrephees basilēes.
sentences.l:
And in it a woman, a housekeeper, bread and wine placed,
and relishes, such as Zeus-nurtured kings eat.
sentences.i: And a woman, the housekeeper, put bread and wine in it, and relishes such as Zeus-nurtured kings eat.
sentences.n: ἐν is an adverb, 'in (it)', the chariot. γυνὴ ταμίη is 'a woman, a housekeeper', the woman in charge of the stores, with the English it has at 2.345. σῖτος is bread. ὄψα are relishes, whatever is eaten with bread, above all meat. οἷα 'such things as' introduces a general statement with the present ἔδουσι 'eat', from the epic verb ἔδω. διοτρεφέες 'Zeus-nurtured' is a standing epithet of kings, whose office comes from Zeus. βασιλῆες is epic for βασιλεῖς.

sentences.t: ἂν δ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχος περικαλλέα βήσετο δίφρον·
sentences.tr: an d’ ara Tēlemachos perikallea bēseto diphron·
sentences.l: And up then Telemachus onto the very beautiful chariot stepped;
sentences.i: Then Telemachus mounted the very beautiful chariot;
sentences.n: ἂν is ἀνά shortened, and it stands apart from βήσετο: tmesis of ἀναβαίνω 'go up, mount'. βήσετο is a 'mixed' aorist middle of βαίνω, with the endings of the imperfect on the aorist stem βησ-. περικαλλέα is 'very beautiful'. δίφρος is properly the platform of the chariot, where the driver and his companion stand, and so the chariot itself.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἄρα Νεστορίδης Πεισίστρατος, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν,
ἐς δίφρον τ’ ἀνέβαινε καὶ ἡνία λάζετο χερσί,
μάστιξεν δ’ ἐλάαν, τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην
ἐς πεδίον, λιπέτην δὲ Πύλου αἰπὺ πτολίεθρον.
sentences.tr:
par d’ ara Nestoridēs Peisistratos, orchamos andrōn,
es diphron t’ anebaine kai hēnia lazeto chersi,
mastixen d’ elaan, tō d’ ouk aekonte petesthēn
es pedion, lipetēn de Pylou aipy ptoliethron.
sentences.l:
and beside him then Nestor’s son Peisistratus, chief of men,
into the chariot mounted, and took the reins in his hands,
and he whipped them to drive on, and the two, not unwilling, flew
into the plain, and they left the steep citadel of Pylos.
sentences.i: and beside him Nestor’s son Peisistratus, chief of men, got into the chariot and took the reins in his hands; he whipped them to drive them on, and the pair flew not unwilling into the plain, and left the steep citadel of Pylos behind.
sentences.n: Νεστορίδης is a patronymic, 'son of Nestor', set before the name. ἀνέβαινε is the imperfect of ἀναβαίνω. ἡνία are the reins, and λάζετο is an unaugmented imperfect of λάζομαι 'take hold of'. μάστιξεν is an unaugmented aorist of μαστίζω 'whip'. ἐλάαν is an epic infinitive of ἐλαύνω, 'to drive them on'. τώ … ἀέκοντε … πετέσθην are duals, 'the two … not unwilling … flew', of the pair of horses; οὐκ ἀέκοντε is an understatement for 'eagerly'. λιπέτην is dual too. αἰπύς is 'steep'.

sentences.t: οἱ δὲ πανημέριοι σεῖον ζυγὸν ἀμφὶς ἔχοντες.
sentences.tr: hoi de panēmerioi seion zygon amphis echontes.
sentences.l: And they all day long shook the yoke, holding it on either side.
sentences.i: All day long the horses shook the yoke that they bore between them.
sentences.n: πανημέριοι 'all day long' is an adjective agreeing with the subject, where English uses an adverb. σεῖον is an unaugmented imperfect of σείω 'shake'. ζυγόν is the yoke, the crossbar laid on the necks of the two horses, and ἀμφὶς ἔχοντες 'holding it on either side' pictures one horse under each end. οἱ is the pronoun, 'they', the horses.

sentences.t:
δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος σκιόωντό τε πᾶσαι ἀγυιαί,
ἐς Φηρὰς δ’ ἵκοντο Διοκλῆος ποτὶ δῶμα,
υἱέος Ὀρτιλόχοιο, τὸν Ἀλφειὸς τέκε παῖδα.
sentences.tr:
dyseto t’ ēelios skioōnto te pasai aguiai,
es Phēras d’ hikonto Dioklēos poti dōma,
huieos Ortilochoio, ton Alpheios teke paida.
sentences.l:
And the sun set, and all the streets grew shadowy,
and to Pherae they came, to the house of Diocles,
son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus begot as his child.
sentences.i: The sun set, and all the streets grew dark, and they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles, son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus begot.
sentences.n: The first line is the same as 2.388 and keeps its English. δύσετο is a mixed aorist of δύω 'sink, set'. σκιόωντο is from σκιάω 'grow shadowy', with the vowel stretched out (Attic ἐσκιῶντο). Pherae lies on the road from Pylos to Lacedaemon. ποτί is an epic form of πρός. Διοκλῆος is the genitive of Diocles. τόν is the relative, Ortilochus, whose father was Alpheus, the river-god; τέκε, an unaugmented aorist, is used of the father begetting, and παῖδα stands in apposition, 'as his son'.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δὲ νύκτ’ ἄεσαν, ὁ δὲ τοῖς πὰρ ξείνια θῆκεν.
sentences.tr: entha de nykt’ aesan, ho de tois par xeinia thēken.
sentences.l: And there they slept the night, and he set beside them the things due to guests.
sentences.i: There they spent the night, and he set before them the hospitality due to guests.
sentences.n: ἔνθα is 'there'. νύκτ’ is an accusative of duration, 'for the night'. ἄεσαν is an aorist, 'slept, passed the night', from a root seen also in ἰαύω 'sleep'. ὁ is Diocles, and τοῖς 'to them'. πὰρ … θῆκεν is tmesis of παρατίθημι 'set beside, set before'. ξείνια are the things due to a guest, entertainment and gifts alike; set 'beside' them, they are most likely the meal.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
ἵππους τε ζεύγνυντ’ ἀνά θ’ ἅρματα ποικίλ’ ἔβαινον·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
hippous te zeugnynt’ ana th’ harmata poikil’ ebainon·
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
both the horses they yoked, and up onto the inlaid chariot they stepped;
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, they yoked the horses and mounted the inlaid chariot;
sentences.n: The dawn formula returns and keeps its English from 2.1 and 404. ἵππους τε … ἀνά θ’ … ἔβαινον joins two actions with τε … τε. ζεύγνυντ’ is ζεύγνυντο, an unaugmented imperfect middle, 'had (the horses) yoked'. ἀνά θ’ … ἔβαινον is tmesis of ἀναβαίνω; θ’ is τε with its τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ἅρματα. ποικίλ’ is ποικίλα 'inlaid, intricately worked', with the English it has for the seat at 1.132.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἔλασαν προθύροιο καὶ αἰθούσης ἐριδούπου·
sentences.tr: ek d’ elasan prothyroio kai aithousēs eridoupou·
sentences.l: and out they drove from the forecourt and the loud-echoing portico;
sentences.i: and drove out of the forecourt and the loud-echoing portico;
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἔλασαν is tmesis of ἐξελαύνω 'drive out', with the genitives giving the place left. ἔλασαν is an unaugmented aorist. The πρόθυρον is the forecourt in front of the house, and the αἴθουσα the roofed portico; ἐριδούπου 'loud-echoing' keeps the fixed English it had at 399, when Telemachus slept in the portico at Pylos. Here it is the portico of Diocles' house.

sentences.t: μάστιξεν δ’ ἐλάαν, τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην.
sentences.tr: mastixen d’ elaan, tō d’ ouk aekonte petesthēn.
sentences.l: and he whipped them to drive on, and the two, not unwilling, flew.
sentences.i: he whipped them to drive them on, and the pair flew not unwilling.
sentences.n: The line is the same as 484 and keeps its English. μάστιξεν is the unaugmented aorist of μαστίζω 'whip'. ἐλάαν is an epic infinitive of ἐλαύνω, 'to drive on': a contracted ἐλᾶν with the vowel stretched out. τώ, ἀέκοντε and πετέσθην are duals, for the pair of horses. οὐκ ἀέκοντε 'not unwilling' is an understatement: the horses run gladly.

sentences.t:
ἷξον δ’ ἐς πεδίον πυρηφόρον, ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα
ἦνον ὁδόν·
sentences.tr:
hixon d’ es pedion pyrēphoron, entha d’ epeita
ēnon hodon·
sentences.l:
And they came to the wheat-bearing plain, and there thereafter
they went on completing their road;
sentences.i: They came to the wheat-bearing plain, and there they pressed on to the end of their road;
sentences.n: ἷξον is an aorist of ἱκνέομαι 'come', formed with -σ- and the endings of the imperfect, and keeps the English it has at 3.31. πεδίον πυρηφόρον is 'the wheat-bearing plain', from πυρός 'wheat' and φέρω 'bear'. ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα is 'and there then'. ἦνον is the imperfect of ἄνω, a by-form of ἀνύω 'accomplish': with ὁδόν it is 'they went on completing their road', pressing on to the end of the stage. γάρ in the next clause gives the reason.

sentences.t: τοῖον γὰρ ὑπέκφερον ὠκέες ἵπποι.
sentences.tr: toion gar hypekpheron ōkees hippoi.
sentences.l: for so well they carried them onward, the swift horses.
sentences.i: for so well did the swift horses carry them on.
sentences.n: τοῖον is an adverbial neuter, 'so, to such a degree': so well, so fast. γάρ gives the reason for the progress of the clause before. ὑπέκφερον is an unaugmented imperfect of ὑπεκφέρω 'carry forward, bear onward', a verb with two preverbs, ὑπό and ἐκ. ὠκέες is the nominative plural of ὠκύς 'swift', and the swift horses of 478 close the sentence.

sentences.t: δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος σκιόωντό τε πᾶσαι ἀγυιαί.
sentences.tr: dyseto t’ ēelios skioōnto te pasai aguiai.
sentences.l: And the sun set, and all the streets grew shadowy.
sentences.i: The sun set, and all the streets grew dark.
sentences.n: The line is the same as 487 and 2.388 and keeps its English, but here it stands alone as a complete sentence and ends with a full stop. The second day's drive ends as the first did, at sundown, and Book 3 ends with it. δύσετο is a mixed aorist of δύω 'set', and σκιόωντο 'grew shadowy' has the vowel stretched out.
